items.title: Challenge is wages, not jobs. Expanding Jan Vishwas interventions can help
items.where: The Editorial Page, page 8 (Manish Sabharwal, Teamlease Services)
items.syllabus: GS3 › Employment; Growth and development · GS2 › Government policies; Transparency and accountability; Citizen-centric governance · GS4 › Probity in governance
items.summary: After decriminalising thousands of offences, the writer argues the next Jan Vishwas phase should make every rule published, knowable and trust-based, because India's problem is low wages, not a lack of jobs.
ideas: Wages, not jobs: India's problem is job quality, not quantity; a third of the workforce is in employed poverty, trapped in informal wage work and self-employment.
GS3 · Employment
India's employment challenge is low-wage informality, not joblessness; the fix lies in formal, high-wage job creation.
Regulatory cholesterol: China's per-capita GDP is five times India's (on par in 1991), not because of effort but because of India's lack of transparency, consistency and trust in law enforcement.
GS3 · Growth / GS2 · Governance
Regulatory cholesterol, not lack of talent or effort, explains much of India's per-capita income gap with China.

Six toxic thought worlds: prior approval (prohibited till permitted), enforcing the unenforceable, process as punishment, blindness to 25+ instruments below Acts, laws for edge cases, and excessive criminalisation.
GS2 · Administrative reform
India's regulatory mindset (prior approval, process as punishment, over-criminalisation) treats the citizen as a suspect.

Three next steps: Siddhant (trust-based regulation on freedom, necessity, proportionality, adopted by 30 million+ civil servants), Sangreh (a single legal record as DPI) and Ashwasan (only published obligations are enforceable).
GS2 · Citizen-centric governance
Jan Vishwas must move from decriminalisation to trust, knowability and certainty through Siddhant, Sangreh and Ashwasan.

Law must be knowable: ignorance of law is no excuse only if the State makes law accessible; earlier attempts failed on design, capacity, fragmented power, attention and technology, and lacked a binding duty to publish.
GS2 · Rule of law / Transparency
A citizen's duty to obey the law presupposes the State's duty to publish it; unpublished rules breed uncertainty and corruption.
keywords: Accumulated rules, filings and permissions that clog enterprise
Regulatory cholesterol raises the cost of formality and pushes firms into informality.
Employed poverty shows India's real problem is wage quality, not job quantity.
A prohibited-till-permitted regime presumes guilt and slows enterprise.
The procedure itself harasses the innocent
When process is punishment, even compliant citizens bear the cost of regulation.
Ignorance of the law is no excuse
Ignorantia juris holds only when the State makes the law knowable.
One machine-readable source for every legal obligation (Sangreh)
A legal DPI like Sangreh can do for compliance what UPI did for payments.
examples: Supreme Court on knowable law
Harla v State of Rajasthan (1952) rejected secret laws; B K Srinivasan (1987) moved to knowability; Viraj Impex (2019) held law operative only when published
GS2 · Judiciary / Rule of law
From Harla (1952) to Viraj Impex (2019), courts have held unpublished law cannot bind citizens.
Global single-source registers
US Federal Register, UK legislation.gov.uk, EU EUR-Lex, Singapore Statutes Online
GS2 · Comparative governance
Democracies like the US, UK and Singapore publish all binding rules in one register; India's Sangreh can follow.
Transparency of Rules Act (TORA)
Sanjeev Sanyal's draft: every enforceable obligation must be published on Sangreh
GS4
GS2 · Transparency / GS4 · Probity
TORA would make publication a precondition for enforcement, curbing discretion and corruption.
Adam Smith and the Constitution
250 years of The Wealth of Nations, 76 of the Constitution: both see government as expanding freedom
GS2 · Constitutional values / Essay
Both Adam Smith and the Constitution see the State as an enabler of freedom, not its gatekeeper.
pyqs: Trust through rule of law: Sangreh and Ashwasan are trust tools.
Job-rich, productive growth: formal high-wage jobs through deregulation.
Informalisation: regulatory cholesterol as a cause.
Civil servant as enabler: Siddhant's adoption by civil servants.

trend.t: Governance questions moved from regulatory autonomy (2015) to the e-governance interactive model (2024) and trust built through rule of law and participation (2026). Employment moved from informalisation (2016) to job-rich, productive growth (2022). GS4 (2025) asks the civil servant to be an enabler, not a regulator.
trend.watch: 'Trust' is the new keyword in GS2 and GS4. Prepare trust-based, citizen-centric governance with examples such as Jan Vishwas, GST arrest powers and self-certification.
focus: Rule of law: knowability of law

potential: "India's challenge is not jobs but wages." Examine, and suggest reforms to promote formal, high-wage employment. (15 marks)
Discuss the significance of the Jan Vishwas initiative for trust-based governance in India. What further reforms are needed? (10 marks)
"The citizen's duty to know the law presupposes the State's duty to make it knowable." Comment. (10 marks)

practice.q: Discuss the significance of the Jan Vishwas initiative for trust-based governance in India. What further reforms are needed?

answer.t: Jan Vishwas has decriminalised thousands of offences, yet a third of India's workforce remains in employed poverty, held back by regulatory cholesterol.

pts.t: The State treats citizens and firms as honest stakeholders, not suspects.
Fewer jail terms for minor lapses reduce the fear of becoming formal.
Less 'process is punishment' lets firms combine land, labour and capital.
Less discretion means fewer chances for rent-seeking.
Fewer petty cases clog courts.
It attacks the root of informality.
Freedom, necessity and proportionality to guide regulation, adopted by 30 million+ civil servants.
One machine-readable legal DPI, unifying gazettes and India Code.
Only published obligations should be enforceable.
Periodic pruning of circulars and rules.

answer.t: Jan Vishwas must move from decriminalisation to certainty, so that what is wrong with India's regulation is fixed by what is right with its democracy.

items.title: Energy security depends on if we electrify, and how we do it
items.where: The Editorial Page, page 8 (Neha Dhingra, CLASP)
items.syllabus: GS3 › Energy infrastructure; Conservation; Industrial policy (MSMEs) · GS2 › Energy security and foreign policy; Statutory bodies (BEE, BIS) · GS1 › Effects of globalisation on Indian society · GS4 › Innovation in public service
items.summary: After the Hormuz disruption hit India's LPG supply, the writer argues that electrifying industrial heat (heat pumps) and kitchens (induction) cuts import exposure, if standards and domestic supply come first.
ideas: A far-off war reached Indian kitchens: when Hormuz shipping stalled in March, families queued for cooking gas; the writer notes India imports about 60% of its LPG, nearly 90% of it via the strait.
GS2 · Energy security / GS1 · Globalisation
India's LPG dependence on one chokepoint shows how a distant conflict becomes a domestic crisis within weeks.

Electrification is a security strategy: in NITI Aayog's net-zero scenario, electricity's share of final energy rises from 21% to 60% by 2070 and the fuel import bill falls from about 4% of GDP to 0.2%.
GS3 · Energy transition
Electrification turns India's clean power base into energy security by replacing imported fuel with domestic electricity.

Industrial heat is the lowest-hanging fruit: factories burn coal, oil and gas on site for much of their energy; electrifying it cuts imports, decarbonises industry and helps exporters meet the EU's CBAM.
GS3 · Industry / Climate
Electrifying industrial heat cuts fuel imports, decarbonises industry and protects exports from carbon border taxes.

How we electrify matters: a heat pump, an air conditioner in reverse, gives 2.5 to 4 units of heat per unit of electricity against at most one from an electric boiler; much MSME heat is below 250°C, within its range.
GS3 · Energy efficiency / MSMEs
Heat pumps meet low-temperature industrial heat with a fraction of the electricity, sparing the grid new capacity.

Cost, confidence and supply hold the market back: high upfront cost, efficiency claims tested under foreign standards, and dependence on Chinese imports; Indian standards, BIS certification and a star label should come before demand surges.
GS3 · Industrial policy / GS2 · Regulatory bodies
Standards and labels before a demand surge, plus domestic manufacturing, keep electrification from importing new dependencies.
keywords: Reliance on one narrow sea route for vital imports
LPG's chokepoint dependence on Hormuz makes cooking fuel a strategic vulnerability.
Switching heat, cooking and transport from fuels to electricity
End-use electrification is how clean power becomes energy security.
Units of heat delivered per unit of electricity
With a coefficient of performance of 2.5 to 4, heat pumps beat electric boilers.
The EU's carbon levy on imports
Electrifying industrial heat helps Indian exporters stay competitive under CBAM.
Mandatory performance norms and star ratings
Standards and labelling build consumer confidence in new technologies.
Swapping fuel imports for equipment imports
Electrification must not swap a fuel dependence for an equipment dependence.
data: Electricity's share of final energy in NITI Aayog's net-zero scenario; fuel import bill falls from about 4% of GDP to 0.2%
NITI Aayog (Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero), via IE
GS3 · Energy transition
NITI Aayog's net-zero scenario raises electricity's share of final energy from 21% to 60% by 2070, cutting the fuel import bill from 4% to 0.2% of GDP.
examples: The March LPG crunch
Hormuz shipping stalled; within weeks families queued for cooking gas and induction cooktops sold out
GS1 · Impact of globalisation · GS2 · Energy security · GS3 · Supply shocks · Essay
Globalisation ties Indian kitchens to distant sea lanes; the March LPG queues show interdependence brings vulnerability as well as access.
BEE star labelling
A simple label turned complex efficiency claims into a signal consumers trust; now needed for heat pumps and induction cooktops
GS4
GS2 · Good governance · GS4 · Innovation in public service · GS3 · Energy efficiency
BEE's star label shows how a simple, trusted public tool changes market behaviour without coercion: governance by information.
pyqs: Energy security challenges and measures: electrification cuts import exposure.
Energy independence through clean technology by 2047.
Energy security and foreign policy in West Asia: the Hormuz shock.
Renewables target and shifting subsidies from fossil fuels.
Affordable, reliable, modern energy for the SDGs.
MSMEs and manufacturing: heat pumps and domestic manufacturing.

trend.t: Energy questions moved from renewable targets and sources (2013, 2015, 2016, 2022) to energy security as a strategic question, in GS2 foreign policy (2017, 2025) and GS3 challenges (2026). The newest asks how clean technology can give energy independence by 2047 (2025).
trend.watch: Energy security came in 2025 and 2026 in both papers, and the angle is shifting from adding supply to cutting dependence. Prepare electrification, efficiency and supply-chain risk together; see also the 31 October E100 card.
focus: Clean-tech manufacturing and dependence on imports

potential: "Electrification is India's most practical route to energy security." Examine with reference to industry and households. (15 marks)
Discuss the potential of heat pumps in decarbonising India's MSME sector. What barriers need to be addressed? (10 marks)
How can standards and labelling accelerate India's energy transition? Illustrate with examples. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Electrification is India's most practical route to energy security." Examine with reference to industry and households.

answer.t: When shipping through Hormuz stalled in March, LPG queues formed and induction cooktops sold out, showing how a distant conflict reaches Indian kitchens.

pts.t: NITI Aayog's net-zero scenario lowers the fuel import bill from about 4% of GDP to 0.2%.
India's clean power base can replace imported fuels.
Factories burning coal, oil and gas on site can switch to electric heat.
Heat pumps give 2.5–4 units of heat per unit of electricity.
Induction diversifies cooking away from LPG.
Cleaner production helps meet the EU's CBAM.
Heat pumps cost more and pay back slowly given high industrial tariffs.
Efficiency claims measured under foreign standards cannot be compared.
Equipment largely imported.
Higher demand needs reliable supply and storage.
Steel and cement need heat beyond heat pumps.
Benefits depend on how clean the grid is.
Indian test standards, BIS certification and a BEE star label.
pts.ex: BEE's star label built trust in appliances.

pts.t: Concessional loans or energy-as-a-service models.
Reduce the cross-subsidy burden on industrial power.
Support for heat pumps and cooktops.
Start with dairy and textile clusters.
Biofuels for diesel uses and strategic reserves.

answer.t: Electrification is the most practical path to energy security, provided India builds standards and factories before demand surges, so it does not swap a fuel dependence for an equipment one.

items.title: In fertiliser sales dip, a lesson for policymakers
items.syllabus: GS3 › Agriculture: inputs, subsidies, food security; Inflation; Effects of climate change · GS1 › Monsoon and El Niño
items.summary: Fertiliser sales fell in April–September as a 'super strong' El Niño weakened the monsoon; the editorial warns of rabi losses and food inflation and asks policymakers to treat climate and geopolitical shocks as the new normal.
ideas: Falling fertiliser sales signal farm distress: sales of all fertilisers, including cheap urea, fell despite higher production and imports, because weak rains gave farmers little reason to apply them.
GS3 · Agriculture inputs
Falling fertiliser offtake despite ample supply is an early indicator of farm distress and lower yields.
El Niño hits both seasons: a deficient monsoon hurt kharif; a dry October and an El Niño expected to persist till early 2027 mean less soil moisture and a warmer winter for rabi.
GS1 · El Niño and monsoon / GS3 · Agriculture
A strong El Niño can hurt both kharif and rabi through deficient rain, low soil moisture and warmer winters.
Climate shocks become food inflation: food inflation has risen sharply this year, and the 2023–24 food-inflation episode was also driven by a long El Niño.
GS3 · Inflation
Food inflation in India is often a weather-driven supply shock that monetary policy alone cannot fix.

Short term, use trade tools: duty-free imports of pulses, raw sugar and cotton till March 31, scrapping customs duty on crude palm and soyabean oil, and a longer window so importers can contract large volumes.
GS3 · Food security / Trade policy
Timely, predictable import windows can cushion domestic shortages and keep food prices stable.

Long term, a 'default reality' mindset: treat climate change and geopolitical tension as baseline conditions; invest in climate-smart breeding, efficient use of water, fertiliser and energy, and reorder an inefficient subsidy regime, which is a political more than an economic challenge.
GS3 · Climate-smart agriculture / Subsidy reform
Treating climate shocks as the default, not the exception, demands climate-smart farming and courageous subsidy reform.
keywords: Unusually intense Pacific warming that weakens India's monsoon
A super-strong El Niño threatens two crop seasons, not one.
Actual use of fertiliser by farmers
Low nutrient offtake today signals lower yields tomorrow.
Prices rising because of output shortfalls, not demand
El Niño-driven food inflation is supply-side, so it needs supply-side answers.
Farming that adapts to and withstands climate stress
Climate-smart breeding and efficient input use make farms resilient to El Niño years.
Planning for shocks as the normal condition
Policy must treat climate and geopolitical shocks as default realities, not rare risks.
More crop per drop, per kg of fertiliser, per unit of energy
Raising input-use efficiency is cheaper and greener than raising input subsidies.
examples: El Niño 2026, the whole chain
Weak monsoon, falling fertiliser sales, risk to rabi, rising food inflation
GS1 · El Niño and monsoon · GS3 · Climate change and food security, inflation · Essay
The 2026 El Niño shows how one ocean-atmosphere event travels from the Pacific to farmers' fields and household food bills.
The repeat of 2023–24
A long El Niño also drove India's last major food-inflation episode
GS3 · Inflation and limits of monetary policy · GS3 · Disaster preparedness
Back-to-back El Niño inflation episodes show climate shocks recur, so preparedness must be permanent.
Imports as a food-security buffer
Duty-free windows for pulses, sugar and edible oils to make up shortfalls
GS1 · Globalisation · GS3 · Food security, trade policy
Calibrated imports show how global markets can buffer domestic climate shocks: a positive face of globalisation.
pyqs: Persistent food inflation and the limits of RBI policy.
Climate change and food security in tropical countries.
Farm subsidies and the WTO Agreement on Agriculture.
Subsidies, cropping pattern and small farmers.

trend.t: Food inflation came first through farm markets (APMCs, 2014) and returned in 2024 as persistent food inflation and the limits of RBI policy. Climate and food security moved from impacts on tropical countries (2023) to climate-smart agriculture (2026). Farm subsidies recur in 2013, 2015, 2017, 2023 and 2026, increasingly with a WTO angle.
trend.watch: Farm subsidies are near-annual, and food inflation and climate-smart agriculture are recent. Prepare one integrated answer: climate shock, then food inflation, then subsidy and trade response.
focus: Supply-side food inflation and limits of monetary policy
Fertiliser subsidy reform and input efficiency

potential: "Food inflation in India is increasingly a climate problem, not a monetary one." Discuss. (15 marks)
How does El Niño affect Indian agriculture across the kharif and rabi seasons? Suggest adaptation measures. (10 marks)
Examine the case for reforming India's fertiliser subsidy regime in the context of climate change. (10 marks)

practice.q: How does El Niño affect Indian agriculture across the kharif and rabi seasons? Suggest adaptation measures.

answer.t: A 'super strong' El Niño this year has weakened the monsoon, and fertiliser sales fell in April–September even as supply rose.

pts.t: Weak rains cut kharif sowing and yields in rainfed regions.
Farmers apply less fertiliser, lowering productivity.
A dry post-monsoon hurts rabi sowing.
Heat at grain-filling reduces wheat yields.
Shortfalls push up prices of pulses, oils and vegetables.
Lower incomes reduce rural demand.
Drought- and heat-tolerant varieties.
Micro-irrigation and soil-health-based fertiliser use.
Timely, predictable duty-free import windows.
Weather-based advisories and crop insurance.
Shift support from inputs to resilience.

answer.t: With El Niño now a recurring visitor, India must plan for climate shocks as the default and build farms that can withstand them.

items.title: Steel policy for 2047 needs to shift focus — from protection to competition
items.where: The Ideas Page, page 9 (Montek S Ahluwalia, Shishir Gupta & Rishita Sachdeva, CSEP)
items.syllabus: GS3 › Industrial policy and its effect on growth; Effects of liberalisation; Mineral resources · GS1 › Distribution of industries and mineral resources; Effects of globalisation · GS2 › Government policies
items.summary: On the Draft National Steel Policy: Vision 2047, the writers argue Indian steel is profitable because it is protected, not efficient, and that duties, quality-control orders and the iron-ore export duty must be phased down.
ideas: Big but not yet competitive: India has risen to the world's second-largest steel producer, but the draft policy's goal of global competitiveness needs a clear meaning, as high profits come from protection, not efficiency.
GS3 · Industrial policy
High profitability under protection is not the same as global competitiveness.
Cheap ore, underpaid states: a 30% export duty on high-grade iron ore keeps domestic ore far below global prices, subsidising steelmakers at the cost of mineral-rich regions and exploration.
GS3 · Mineral policy / GS1 · Resource regions
Export duties on ore transfer value from mineral-rich regions to steelmakers and discourage mining.
Protection hurts users of steel: import duties and Quality Control Orders make Indian steel costlier than even high-cost Japan, raising costs for construction, automobiles and export-oriented MSMEs.
GS3 · Industry / MSMEs
Protecting an input industry taxes every industry that uses it, especially MSME exporters.

Competition did not kill other industries: tariff cuts in pharmaceuticals and auto components were followed by rising shares in global exports; steel should cut duties to ASEAN levels over five years and drop QCOs.
GS3 · Liberalisation / Trade
Pharma and auto parts show that lower protection can raise, not reduce, export competitiveness.

Reform the structure, not just tariffs: consider privatising some public-sector plants, remove the ore export duty and overhaul mining policy that discourages exploration (explorers must surrender discovered mines to auction).
GS3 · PSU reform / Mining
Competitive steel needs privatisation of laggard PSUs and a mining policy that rewards exploration.
keywords: Protection that outlives its purpose and blunts efficiency
Steel risks an infant-industry trap: protected long after it grew up.
Quality Control Orders that restrict imports without tariffs
Quality Control Orders act as non-tariff barriers that raise input costs.
Protection of an industry net of protection on its inputs
High effective protection for steel shifts costs to downstream users.
Cost advantage of industries that use an input
Cheaper steel improves downstream competitiveness in construction and autos.
Reward to finders of new mineral deposits
Without exploration incentives, India's geological potential stays largely unexplored.
data: 45 Mt
Steel export target in the Draft National Steel Policy: Vision 2047
Ministry of Steel, via IE
GS3 · Industrial policy
The Draft National Steel Policy targets 45 million tonnes of steel exports by 2047.
Steel products under QCOs / recommended for removal by the Gauba Committee / actually suspended so far
Gauba Committee (reported), via IE
GS3 · Trade / Ease of doing business
QCOs cover 228 steel products; the Gauba Committee reportedly recommended removing 122, but only 59 have been suspended.
examples: Pharma and auto components after tariff cuts
Lower protection was followed by higher shares in global exports
GS3 · Liberalisation · GS1 · Globalisation
Pharma and auto parts show that exposure to competition can make Indian industry globally competitive.
Quality Control Orders on steel
Rules meant for quality working as import barriers
GS4
GS3 · Ease of doing business · GS2 · Regulatory overreach
QCOs on steel show how a well-meant regulation can turn into protection and raise costs for small firms.
Iron-ore export duty
Domestic steelmakers gain while mineral-rich states earn less
GS1 · Resource regions · GS2 · Federalism · GS3 · Mining
The iron-ore export duty shows how national policy can quietly shift value away from mineral-rich states.
Jamsetji Tata, 1912
Built India's first steel plant despite British scorn, without today's protections
GS1 · Modern Indian history · Essay
Jamsetji Tata's steel plant shows Indian enterprise succeeding on capability, not protection.
pyqs: Why industrial growth lagged GDP growth after reforms, and recent industrial policy.
Challenges as the world turns to protectionism.
Manufacturing and MSMEs in faster growth.
Why mining contributes little to India's GDP.
Location of iron and steel industries.

trend.t: Industry questions moved from why manufacturing lagged after reforms (2017) and capital-intensive exports (2017) to manufacturing and MSMEs for faster growth (2023) and a world turning protectionist (2018, 2025). Geography asks about steel location (2014, 2020) and mining's low share in GDP (2021).
trend.watch: Protectionism and manufacturing competitiveness have come in 2018, 2023 and 2025. Prepare the trade-off between protecting industry and making it competitive, with sector examples.
focus: Protection vs competitiveness in industrial policy

potential: "Protection may raise profits, but only competition builds global competitiveness." Examine with reference to India's steel sector. (15 marks)
Why does mining contribute little to India's GDP despite rich mineral resources? Suggest reforms. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Protection may raise profits, but only competition builds global competitiveness." Examine with reference to India's steel sector.

answer.t: India is now the world's second-largest steel producer, and the Draft National Steel Policy targets 45 Mt of exports by 2047, yet its profits rest heavily on protection.

pts.t: Shielded the industry while it scaled up.
Steel underpins defence and infrastructure.
Protects against surges of cheap imports.
Supports jobs in steel regions.
Assured margins attracted capital.
Export duty on ore underpays mineral-rich regions.
Steel costlier than in Japan, hurting construction and autos.
Higher input prices blunt export competitiveness.
QCOs on 228 products; only 59 suspended of 122 recommended.
Profits mask inefficiency, especially in PSUs.
Mining rules discourage new discoveries.
Bring duties to ASEAN levels over five years.
As the Gauba Committee recommended.
Expose firms to global ore prices.
Privatise laggard plants with strategic oversight.
Reward explorers, as in Australia.
Lower protection went with higher export shares.

answer.t: As pharma and auto parts show, Indian industry competes best when exposed to the world; steel's road to 2047 must run from protection to competition.

items.title: Why Delhi mustn't take its eyes off Pakistan-Maldives
items.where: The Ideas Page, page 9 (Aditya Gowdara Shivamurthy, ORF)
items.syllabus: GS2 › India and its neighbourhood; Bilateral, regional and global groupings · GS3 › Security challenges; Maritime security
items.summary: Maldives President Muizzu's state visit to Pakistan, with 20 MoUs including defence, shows the Maldives diversifying beyond India; the writer backs India's economic approach but says it must state its security red lines.
ideas: Diversification beyond India: Muizzu's visit produced 20 MoUs, from socio-economic sectors to cybersecurity, drugs and defence and maritime security, and a plan to scale up trade.
GS2 · India–Maldives
Small neighbours are hedging by diversifying partners, testing India's primacy in its neighbourhood.
A crowded defence space: the Maldives also has defence MoUs with China and Turkey, has bought armoured vehicles from the UAE and joined a Saudi-led maritime coalition.
GS2 · Neighbourhood / GS3 · Maritime security
Multiple defence partners for the Maldives crowd the Indian Ocean Region close to India's maritime boundaries.

Pakistan's wider play: since Operation Sindoor, Pakistan and China have held trilaterals with Bangladesh and Afghanistan; Pakistan has pushed SAARC revival, a South Asian bloc without India and a larger naval presence in the Bay of Bengal.
GS2 · Regional groupings
Pakistan is using new regional formats to dilute India's centrality in South Asia.

India's pragmatic economic diplomacy: T-bill extensions, debt restructuring, credit lines and currency swaps build leverage and goodwill without fuelling anti-India nationalism ahead of Maldivian elections.
GS2 · Neighbourhood First / Economic diplomacy
India's economic support builds leverage while avoiding the nationalist backlash that pressure would provoke.
Clear red lines on security: some MoUs (cybercrime, drugs) may even help India, but defence ties with Pakistan need clear communication of India's concerns.
GS2 · Foreign policy / GS3 · Security
India can accept the Maldives' diversification but must draw red lines on defence and security.
keywords: Small states balancing among several powers
The Maldives' outreach to Pakistan, China and Turkey is classic strategic hedging.
India's policy priority for its immediate neighbours
Neighbourhood First relies on economic support to keep small neighbours close.
Using credit, aid and swaps to shape relations
India's currency swaps and credit lines to the Maldives are economic statecraft.
Limits a country signals it will not accept
India must communicate red lines on Pakistan's defence role in the Maldives.
More extra-regional powers active in the Indian Ocean
A crowded IOR raises India's maritime security challenges.
data: $13 million → $200 million
Maldives–Pakistan trade target for the next two years
Maldives–Pakistan agreements during the state visit, via IE
GS2 · India's neighbourhood
The Maldives and Pakistan aim to raise trade from $13 million to $200 million in two years.
examples: India's support to the Maldives
T-bill extensions, debt restructuring, credit lines and currency swaps
GS2 · Neighbourhood First, economic diplomacy, soft power
India's financial support to the Maldives shows economic statecraft winning goodwill without coercion.
Muizzu's defence MoUs with Pakistan, China, Turkey
A small state spreading its security partnerships
GS2 · Small-state hedging · GS3 · Maritime security
The Maldives' multiple defence MoUs show small states hedging among powers in a crowded Indian Ocean.
Pakistan's South Asian bloc idea
A proposed regional bloc without India
GS2 · Regional groupings (SAARC)
Pakistan's push for a bloc without India shows regionalism being used to isolate a neighbour.
pyqs: Geopolitical and geostrategic importance of the Maldives for India.
Political developments in the Maldives and concerns for India.
BRI turning South Asia into a theatre of great-power competition.
How domestic factors shape foreign policy (India–Sri Lanka).
Pakistan and the future of SAARC.

trend.t: The Maldives was asked in 2013 for its political turmoil and in 2024 for its geostrategic importance to trade, energy and maritime security. Neighbourhood questions moved from domestic factors in foreign policy (2013) and SAARC (2016) to China's BRI turning South Asia into a theatre of competition (2026).
trend.watch: The Maldives has been asked twice, and island neighbours keep returning through maritime security. Prepare small-state hedging, India's economic diplomacy and extra-regional powers in the IOR.
focus: Pakistan and China in South Asian groupings

potential: "India's neighbourhood policy must balance economic generosity with clear security red lines." Discuss with reference to the Maldives. (10 marks)
Examine the implications of growing Maldives–Pakistan defence ties for India's maritime security. (10 marks)

practice.q: "India's neighbourhood policy must balance economic generosity with clear security red lines." Discuss with reference to the Maldives.
parts: Security red lines: why they matter

answer.t: Maldives President Muizzu's state visit to Pakistan produced 20 MoUs, including on defence and maritime security, even as India has extended credit lines and currency swaps to Malé.

pts.t: T-bill extensions, credit lines and swaps keep India the first responder.
Coercion would feed anti-India politics before elections.
Cooperation on cybercrime and drugs helps India too.
Defence MoUs with Pakistan, China and Turkey bring rivals closer.
A bloc without India and a larger naval presence.
The Maldives sits astride key sea lanes.

pts.k: Communicate red lines privately and clearly
pts.t: On defence presence and bases.
Health, connectivity and climate resilience.
Coast-guard and maritime-domain-awareness links.

answer.t: India should stay the Maldives' most generous partner while making clear that its security in the Indian Ocean is not negotiable.

items.title: Chopper operators in Uttarakhand protest mandatory co-pilot rule
items.where: Nation, page 7 (Vidheesha Kuntamalla); see also Explained, page 11, on recurring helicopter accidents
items.syllabus: GS2 › Statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies (DGCA) · GS3 › Infrastructure: airways; Disaster management
items.summary: Minor topic: after a helicopter crash near Joshimath killed six, the DGCA made two pilots mandatory on Char Dham flights; 11 operators say the cost makes services unviable.
ideas: Regulator reacts to a crash: two days after a Char Dham helicopter crash killed all six on board, the DGCA made two pilots mandatory on every flight and required control-room clearance before each leg.
GS2 · Regulatory bodies
A regulator's job is to tighten safety norms when risks are exposed, even at a cost to operators.
Safety vs viability: 11 operators told the DGCA that higher crew, accommodation and logistics costs cannot be absorbed or fully passed on, and threatened to suspend charter services.
GS2 · Regulation / GS3 · Air transport
Safety regulation must weigh compliance costs, or services may shrink or shift to riskier informal operators.
Consultation matters: operators asked for a mutually workable solution; rules made after consultation are more likely to be followed.
GS2 · Regulatory governance
Consultative rule-making balances public safety with the viability of regulated businesses.
keywords: Regulators too close to industry, or imposing costs without balance
Good regulation avoids both capture by operators and overreach that kills services.

Mountain flying in bad weather calls for risk-based regulation, not uniform norms.

Mandatory co-pilot and control-room clearance after a fatal crash

items.title: How welfare board will function, what changes for unorganised, gig workers
items.where: Economy, page 10 (Ravi Dutta Mishra & Aanchal Magazine)
items.syllabus: GS3 › Employment; Labour reforms · GS2 › Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections; Statutory bodies
items.summary: Follow-up: the Labour Ministry has notified two social security boards (40 members for unorganised workers, 22 for gig and platform workers) under the Code on Social Security.
evolution: Labour Ministry notifies the National Social Security Board under the Code on Social Security (Economy, page 23).
Details: two boards, aggregator contributions to a social security fund, and EPFO coverage widened.
ideas: Two boards, not one: a 40-member board for unorganised workers and a 22-member board for gig and platform workers, which includes aggregators such as quick-commerce and delivery platforms.
GS2 · Statutory bodies
Separate boards recognise that gig and platform workers need schemes designed for platform work.
Who pays: aggregators must contribute 1–2% of annual turnover to a social security fund, capped at 5% of what they pay workers; the fund also draws on governments, CSR and fines.
GS3 · Labour / GS2 · Welfare
Aggregator contributions put part of the cost of gig workers' security on the platforms that profit from them.
What it covers: schemes for life and disability cover, accident insurance, health and maternity benefits, old-age protection and crèches.
GS2 · Welfare
Social security for gig workers spans life-cycle risks, from maternity to old age.
Wider formal coverage: EPFO provisions now apply to all establishments with 20 or more employees, regardless of industry, not only those in the old schedule.
GS3 · Labour reforms
Extending EPFO to all establishments with 20+ workers widens formal social security.
keywords: Pooled fund for unorganised, gig and platform workers
A dedicated Social Security Fund gives gig workers' schemes a stable financing base.
Platforms paying a share of turnover towards workers' welfare
The aggregator levy shares the cost of social protection with platforms.
data: 1–2% of turnover (cap 5%)
Aggregators' contribution to the social security fund, capped at 5% of amounts payable to workers
Code on Social Security, via IE
GS3 · Labour / GS2 · Welfare
Aggregators must contribute 1–2% of turnover to gig workers' social security, capped at 5% of payouts (Code on Social Security).
examples: Aggregators on the gig workers' board
Platforms sit with worker bodies to design welfare schemes
GS2 · Tripartism, statutory bodies · GS3 · Digital economy
Putting aggregators and worker bodies on one board shows tripartism adapting to the platform economy.
pyqs: The gig economy and women's empowerment.

items.title: Retirement fund body unveils services to ease provident fund access; Digi Yatra trials for overseas flyers
items.where: Economy, page 10 (ENS Economic Bureau; Briefly, PTI)
items.syllabus: GS2 › E-governance: applications, models, successes; Citizen-centric governance · GS4 › Empathy and compassion in public service
items.summary: Minor topic: EPFO launched verified WhatsApp services and automatic settlement of small inoperative accounts; Digi Yatra trials for international passengers began at seven airports.
ideas: Services where people already are: EPFO's verified WhatsApp service gives PF balance, transactions and passbook, and guidance on the Employment Linked Incentive scheme, reducing office visits.
GS2 · E-governance
Delivering services on familiar platforms like WhatsApp makes e-governance truly citizen-centric.
From claims to automatic delivery: Aadhaar-verified inoperative EPF accounts with balances up to ₹1,000 will be settled without individual claims.
GS2 · Citizen-centric governance
Automatic settlement shifts the burden from the citizen to the State, the essence of proactive governance.
Human sensitivity in social security: the Labour Minister said every worker's grievance must be met with compassion and empathy, treating workers as nation-builders.
GS4 · Empathy in public service
Social security administration must combine efficiency with empathy for the worker.
Paperless travel goes international: Digi Yatra trials for Indian e-passport holders on select international flights have begun at seven airports, with wider rollout expected in 2027.
GS2 · E-governance / GS3 · Infrastructure
Digi Yatra shows digital public infrastructure extending from domestic to international travel.
keywords: No-claim settlement is proactive delivery: the State reaches the citizen first.
Services on platforms citizens already use
WhatsApp-based services improve last-mile digital access.
examples: EPFO WhatsApp and auto-settlement
Verified WhatsApp services; small inoperative accounts settled without claims

GS2 · E-governance, citizen-centric governance · GS4 · Innovation and empathy in public service
EPFO's WhatsApp service and no-claim settlement show innovation in public service that saves citizens time and trips.

Trials at Delhi, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Cochin, Mumbai, Chennai and Amritsar

ethics.title: The State's duty to be knowable
ethics.news: A writer proposes that only rules published on one national legal register should be enforceable against citizens.
ethics.syllabus: Transparency; Rule of law; Probity in governance; Trust
ethics.link: A government that enforces rules citizens cannot find betrays fairness; publishing every obligation is an ethical duty that limits discretion and corruption.
ethics.question: "Hidden rules are the soil in which corruption grows." Discuss.

ethics.title: Generosity without coercion
ethics.news: As the Maldives signs defence MoUs with Pakistan, India continues credit lines and currency swaps and avoids pressure that could fuel anti-India nationalism.
ethics.syllabus: Ethical issues in international relations: respect for sovereignty, prudence and national interest
ethics.link: Respecting a small neighbour's sovereign choices while protecting one's own security shows prudence in IR: interest pursued without domination.
ethics.question: "A large power earns influence over small neighbours through generosity, not pressure." Discuss from an ethical perspective.

ethics.title: A lifelong home: CSR with care
ethics.news: Reliance Foundation announced a 100-acre township near Mumbai as a lifelong home for orphaned children, senior citizens and persons with disabilities, in family-style homes with caregivers.
ethics.syllabus: Ethics in business: corporate social responsibility; Compassion towards the weaker sections
ethics.link: CSR is most meaningful when it meets a lasting social need with dignity, here the anxiety of parents of children with disabilities about who will care for them; the test is sustained care, not announcement.
ethics.question: "Corporate social responsibility is an ethical commitment, not merely a legal obligation." Discuss with examples.

essay.title: Hammurabi's eye for an eye
essay.text: In Hammurabi's code, blinding an aristocrat cost you an eye, but blinding a slave cost only a fine: punishment reflected power, not principle. Sabharwal sees the same disease in regulation today: show me the employer, and I'll show you the rule.
essay.use: For 'A society that has more justice is a society that needs less charity' (2023) and 'There can be no social justice without economic prosperity, but economic prosperity without social justice is meaningless' (2020).

essay.title: A war far away, a queue at the gas agency
essay.text: When shipping through the Strait of Hormuz stalled in March, Indian families queued for cooking gas and induction cooktops sold out within weeks: a conflict thousands of kilometres away had reached the kitchen.
essay.use: For 'Alternative technologies for a climate change resilient India' (2018) and 'Technology as the silent factor in international relations' (2020).

essay.title: Hard choices on subsidies
essay.text: Facing a 'super strong' El Niño, the editorial says India must treat climate change and geopolitical tension as default realities and reorder its inefficient subsidy regime, a challenge it calls political more than economic.
essay.use: For 'Shelving hard decisions is the least ethical course' (2026) and 'We may brave human laws but cannot resist natural laws' (2017).

essay.title: Jamsetji Tata's steel plant
essay.text: When Jamsetji Tata applied to the imperial government in 1912 to set up a steel plant, a British official sneered that Indians simply could not do it. Permission was given and Tata succeeded. Today, writers ask whether he would have wanted the mix of duties and quality-control orders that now shield Indian steel.
essay.use: For 'A ship in harbour is safe, but that is not what a ship is for' (2022) and 'Courage to accept and dedication to improve are two keys to success' (2019).
